chapter: Paris, the Blackbirds and Noble Sissle
title: Joe Keyes's grievance and death in New York
summary: Trumpeter Joe Keyes, hired from Jap Allen's band in Kansas City, quarrelled with Sissle over pay and was later found dead in the East River.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: I told him, I said, 'Wire Joe,' Joe Smith, and he wired Joe, and Wendell Culley.
Right.
And, who was the other trumpet player, I don't know. But we had a -- I had a sad awakening, after coming back to Paris, with Sissle in 1930.
The third trumpet player that we had with us, who was really a second trumpet player, Joe Keyes -- you heard of him?
I've heard the name, yes.
He was wonderful, a wonderful trumpet player. We met him in Kansas City. He was with Jap Allen's orchestra.
Jap Allen's orchestra?
Yeh. You've heard of him, --
Briggs
Sure.

And he left Jap Allen's orchestra to travel with us. And when we got to New York, apparently he claimed, it surprised me ever so much, he said to me, "Briggs," he said, "What kind of man is this Sissle?" I said, "He's okay.with me," I said, "So far," and I said, "With all the boys, Buster, and Ralph, Duches and he and everyone else, so we never had any complaints about him."
So, he said, "Well, he promised to pay me a certain price, and he didn't live up to his promise." He said, "Look, Briggs, his head is worth ten cents a pound to me." (Laughter).
Really.
And that's a terrific expression; isn't it?
Yes.
So, I said, "Now, look, Joe," I said, "Just calm down and get
Briggs 226

yourself together." I said, "Mr. Sissle, if you have any misunderstanding with him, I said, you can just go ahead and thrash it out with him, he's a fine person." And, adding onto that, I said, "He is not broke." MR. COLLIER: Right. MR. BRIGGS: So, whatever happened, I don't know. but he didn't come back to Paris, with us, he didn't come back to Paris. He decided not to take him to Paris, because automatically Sissle could have taken him and whipped the band into -- whipped him into shape to replace me. MR. COLLIER: Right. MR. BRIGGS: Sissle knew I wasn't going back with his orchestra. And he didn't, so I, we came back to Paris, and a few months after I had a letter from a friend saying that --
Briggs
his mother had sent -- he was in pretty bad shape in New York. New York is a pretty bad place to be broke, you know.
He had sent his mother, money, and she sent him money for his ticket on Greyhound Bus back to Kansas City, and $300.
And apparently he went around to some gin mill or something, flashing his money, and drinking and drinking, and they found his body in the East River.
They found his body in the East River?
Yes. Too bad, huh.
Oh boy.
Yeh. He was a fine boy. A nice boy if you could -- he had plenty of sense, maybe he -- I didn't know whether he smoked, but he might of, we called it "tea" in those days.
Right.
Briggs 228
I don't know, I don't know what happened with Joe Keyes. And he was a terrific trumpet player. Very good trumpet player.
